This is Task Factory, our entry for Innodata Track 1, the Coding Task Factory. The question it answers: how do you automatically generate realistic feature-development tasks, with a reference solution, hidden tests, and evidence that those tests are actually good. We ran it on three real repositories: click in Python, jsoncpp in C plus plus, and zod in TypeScript.

This is the Atlas. Each glowing orb is one generated task. There are nineteen validated tasks across five feature families. Every task is pinned to a base commit, so it is reproducible. The key idea is rule algebra: a task is a sampled set of independent behavioural rules. The requirements, the implementation, and the tests are all derived from the same rules, so they cannot drift apart.

Now we fly into one task and replay its validation. A packet passes through seven gates. S1: the new tests fail on the base commit. S2: the reference solution passes them. S3: the repository's existing test suite still passes. S4: every single rule is detected. S5: mutation testing. S6: a regression guard on neighbouring code. And S7: the result is deterministic. Each gate shows real evidence, not a claim.

Here is the strongest check. We remove one rule at a time from the implementation, and the tests that belong to that rule turn red. That proves every requirement in the problem statement is independently tested, and that a solution which forgets a requirement will be caught.

Now the grader. Applying the reference solution to the pinned commit, with the hidden tests, gives resolved. All fifty seven feature tests pass, and all two thousand six hundred fifty three existing tests still pass. This is a real run of the real test suite, happening live.

Next, a plausible but incomplete solution that forgets one rule. The grader marks it unresolved, and shows exactly which requirement failed, so the task measures partial progress instead of a single pass or fail.
And if a candidate tries to cheat by editing the tests, the grader rejects it outright.

The variation view answers the question of whether tasks are really different. Each bar shows how well one task's tests pass against another task's reference solution. The gold diagonal is each task against itself. Everything off the diagonal is lower, in some families close to zero, which shows the tasks differ in behaviour and not just in wording.

The lab lets you tick any combination of rules and build a brand new task live. The factory generates it, validates it through the same gates, and packages it. The result: nineteen tasks, all valid, with mutation kill rates between eighty one and one hundred percent. Everything is repeatable from one command line, and our limitations are documented honestly in the repository. Thank you.
